text: David Peter Robbins (12 August 1942 in Brooklyn – 4 September 2003 in Princeton) was an American mathematician. He is best known for introducing alternating sign matrices and for his work on generalizations of Heron's formula related to the area of polygons, leading to the naming of Robbins pentagons—cyclic pentagons with integer side lengths and areas—after him. Robbins grew up in Manhattan and attended the Fieldston School. He studied at Harvard, where his undergraduate advisor was Andrew Gleason, and later pursued graduate studies at MIT. After teaching at Fieldston during a hiatus, he completed his Ph.D. in 1970. He taught at MIT, Phillips Exeter Academy, Hamilton College, and Washington and Lee University. In 1980, he moved to Princeton, New Jersey, where he worked at the Institute for Defense Analyses Center for Communications Research until his death from pancreatic cancer. A symposium in his honor was held in June 2003, and the proceedings were published as a special issue of Advances in Applied Mathematics. In 2005, the Mathematical Association of America established the David P. Robbins Prize, awarded every three years to one or more researchers in algebra, combinatorics, or discrete mathematics; the first recipient in 2008 was Neil Sloane for his work on the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. The American Mathematical Society also has a prize named after him, the David P. Robbins Prize (AMS), with the first winners being Samuel P. Ferguson and Thomas C. Hales for their work on the Kepler conjecture.
